options.B: An election symbol is a flag used by the government
options.C: An election symbol is a logo of the Election Commission
options.D: An election symbol is a national emblem

questions.explanation: An election symbol is a visual sign allotted or reserved for a political party or candidate under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is a party manifesto?

options.A: A party manifesto is a document setting out a political party's stated policies, priorities and proposed programmes for voters
options.B: A party manifesto is a list of party members
options.C: A party manifesto is a list of election symbols
options.D: A party manifesto is a list of election expenses

questions.explanation: A party manifesto is a document setting out a political party's stated policies, priorities and proposed programmes for voters.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is anti-defection law?

options.A: Anti-defection law provides grounds on which members of Parliament or State Legislatures may be disqualified for defection, under the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution
options.B: Anti-defection law provides grounds for disqualification of the President
options.C: Anti-defection law provides grounds for disqualification of judges
options.D: Anti-defection law provides grounds for disqualification of civil servants

questions.explanation: Anti-defection law provides grounds on which members of Parliament or State Legislatures may be disqualified for defection, under the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: Which Constitutional Amendment introduced the anti-defection law?

options.A: The 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985
options.B: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976
options.C: The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978
options.D: The 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988

questions.explanation: The 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985 introduced the anti-defection law.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: Which schedule contains the anti-defection provisions?

options.A: The Tenth Schedule
options.B: The Ninth Schedule
options.C: The Eleventh Schedule
options.D: The Twelfth Schedule

questions.explanation: The Tenth Schedule contains the anti-defection provisions.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is a whip in parliamentary practice?

options.A: A whip is a party instruction to its legislators about attendance or voting on specified matters; disobeying a valid party direction may have consequences under the anti-defection framework
options.B: A whip is a constitutional body
options.C: A whip is a judicial order
options.D: A whip is an election symbol

questions.explanation: A whip is a party instruction to its legislators about attendance or voting on specified matters; disobeying a valid party direction may have consequences under the anti-defection framework.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is the difference between a political party and a pressure group?

options.A: A political party seeks to gain or exercise governmental power, commonly through elections; a pressure group seeks to influence public policy without necessarily seeking to form the government
options.B: A political party seeks to influence policy; a pressure group seeks to form government
options.C: There is no difference between them
options.D: A political party is a constitutional body; a pressure group is a statutory body

questions.explanation: A political party seeks to gain or exercise governmental power, commonly through elections; a pressure group seeks to influence public policy without necessarily seeking to form the government.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is an election?

options.A: An election is a formal process through which voters choose representatives or decide an issue by casting votes
options.B: An election is a process through which the judiciary appoints representatives
options.C: An election is a process through which the military appoints representatives
options.D: An election is a process through which the monarch appoints representatives

questions.explanation: An election is a formal process through which voters choose representatives or decide an issue by casting votes.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is an electoral system?

options.A: An electoral system is the set of rules that converts votes into elected offices or legislative seats
options.B: An electoral system is a political party
options.C: An electoral system is a constitutional body
options.D: An electoral system is a pressure group

questions.explanation: An electoral system is the set of rules that converts votes into elected offices or legislative seats.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is the First-Past-the-Post (FPTP) system?

options.A: Under FPTP, the candidate who receives more votes than any other candidate in a constituency wins, even without securing an absolute majority
options.B: Under FPTP, the candidate who receives an absolute majority wins
options.C: Under FPTP, seats are allocated in proportion to votes received
options.D: Under FPTP, the candidate is elected by the legislature

questions.explanation: Under FPTP, the candidate who receives more votes than any other candidate in a constituency wins, even without securing an absolute majority.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: Which electoral system is used for direct elections to the Lok Sabha and most State Legislative Assemblies?

options.A: The First-Past-the-Post system
options.B: Proportional representation
options.C: Single transferable vote
options.D: Mixed member proportional representation

questions.explanation: The First-Past-the-Post system is used for direct elections to the Lok Sabha and most State Legislative Assemblies.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is proportional representation?

options.A: Proportional representation is an electoral approach designed to allocate seats broadly in proportion to the votes received by parties or candidates
options.B: Proportional representation is a system in which the candidate with the most votes wins
options.C: Proportional representation is a system in which the candidate is elected by the legislature
options.D: Proportional representation is a system in which only the wealthy can vote

questions.explanation: Proportional representation is an electoral approach designed to allocate seats broadly in proportion to the votes received by parties or candidates.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: Which method is used to elect the President of India?

options.A: Proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote, using an electoral college and secret ballot
options.B: First-Past-the-Post system
options.C: Direct popular vote
options.D: Nomination by the Prime Minister

questions.explanation: The President of India is elected by proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote, using an electoral college and secret ballot.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: Which method is used to elect Rajya Sabha members representing States?

options.A: Proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote, through elected members of the respective State Legislative Assemblies
options.B: First-Past-the-Post system
options.C: Direct popular vote
options.D: Nomination by the Governor

questions.explanation: Rajya Sabha members representing States are elected by proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote, through elected members of the respective State Legislative Assemblies.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is the single transferable vote (STV)?

options.A: STV is a preferential voting method in which voters rank candidates and votes may transfer according to preferences to help elect candidates who reach the required quota
options.B: STV is a system in which the candidate with the most votes wins
options.C: STV is a system in which voters can only vote for one candidate
options.D: STV is a system in which the legislature elects the President

questions.explanation: STV is a preferential voting method in which voters rank candidates and votes may transfer according to preferences to help elect candidates who reach the required quota.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is universal adult suffrage in India?

options.A: Every Indian citizen aged 18 or above is entitled to be registered as an elector, subject to constitutional and statutory disqualifications
options.B: Every Indian citizen aged 21 or above is entitled to vote
options.C: Only property owners are entitled to vote
options.D: Only men are entitled to vote

questions.explanation: Under universal adult suffrage in India, every Indian citizen aged 18 or above is entitled to be registered as an elector, subject to constitutional and statutory disqualifications.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: Which article provides for elections to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies on the basis of adult suffrage?

options.A: Article 326
options.B: Article 324
options.C: Article 325
options.D: Article 327

questions.explanation: Article 326 provides for elections to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies on the basis of adult suffrage.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: Which amendment reduced the voting age from 21 to 18 years?

options.A: The 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988
options.B: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976
options.C: The 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978
options.D: The 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985

questions.explanation: The 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988 reduced the voting age from 21 to 18 years.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: When is National Voters' Day observed in India?

options.A: 25 January
options.B: 26 January
options.C: 15 August
options.D: 2 October

questions.explanation: National Voters' Day is observed on 25 January, the foundation day of the Election Commission of India.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: When was the Election Commission of India established?

options.A: 25 January 1950
options.B: 26 January 1950
options.C: 26 November 1949
options.D: 15 August 1947

questions.explanation: The Election Commission of India was established on 25 January 1950.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is the constitutional status of the Election Commission of India?

options.A: It is an independent constitutional authority under Article 324
options.B: It is a statutory body under the Representation of the People Act
options.C: It is an executive body under the Ministry of Law
options.D: It is a judicial body under the Supreme Court

questions.explanation: The Election Commission of India is an independent constitutional authority under Article 324.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: Which elections are conducted by the Election Commission of India?

options.A: Elections to Parliament, State Legislative Assemblies and the offices of President and Vice-President
options.B: Elections to Panchayats and Municipalities
options.C: Elections to cooperative societies
options.D: Elections to trade unions

questions.explanation: The Election Commission of India conducts elections to Parliament, State Legislative Assemblies and the offices of President and Vice-President.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: Who conducts elections to Panchayats and Municipalities?

options.A: The State Election Commission of the respective State, under Articles 243K and 243ZA
options.B: The Election Commission of India
options.C: The Union Public Service Commission
options.D: The Finance Commission

questions.explanation: The State Election Commission of the respective State conducts elections to Panchayats and Municipalities, under Articles 243K and 243ZA.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is the Model Code of Conduct?

options.A: The Model Code of Conduct is a set of guidelines issued by the Election Commission to regulate the conduct of political parties and candidates during elections; it is not itself a comprehensive statute
options.B: The Model Code of Conduct is a constitutional amendment
options.C: The Model Code of Conduct is a law passed by Parliament
options.D: The Model Code of Conduct is a judicial order

questions.explanation: The Model Code of Conduct is a set of guidelines issued by the Election Commission to regulate the conduct of political parties and candidates during elections; it is not itself a comprehensive statute.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is an electoral roll?

options.A: An electoral roll is the official list of persons registered as eligible voters in a particular constituency
options.B: An electoral roll is a list of candidates contesting elections
options.C: An electoral roll is a list of election symbols
options.D: An electoral roll is a list of polling booths

questions.explanation: An electoral roll is the official list of persons registered as eligible voters in a particular constituency.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is a constituency?

options.A: A constituency is a defined geographical electoral area from which voters elect a representative
options.B: A constituency is a political party
options.C: A constituency is an election symbol
options.D: A constituency is a polling booth

questions.explanation: A constituency is a defined geographical electoral area from which voters elect a representative.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is delimitation?

options.A: Delimitation is the process of redrawing the boundaries of electoral constituencies and, where legally provided, readjusting seat allocation
options.B: Delimitation is the process of registering voters
options.C: Delimitation is the process of counting votes
options.D: Delimitation is the process of allotting election symbols

questions.explanation: Delimitation is the process of redrawing the boundaries of electoral constituencies and, where legally provided, readjusting seat allocation.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is a by-election?

options.A: A by-election is an election held to fill a vacancy that arises before the normal end of a representative body's term
options.B: A by-election is a general election held after the term of a representative body ends
options.C: A by-election is an election held for the office of the President
options.D: A by-election is an election held for local bodies only

questions.explanation: A by-election is an election held to fill a vacancy that arises before the normal end of a representative body's term.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is NOTA?

options.A: NOTA means 'None of the Above'; it allows an elector to register that they do not wish to vote for any of the listed candidates
options.B: NOTA means 'National Online Voting Application'
options.C: NOTA means 'New Official Training Academy'
options.D: NOTA means 'National Optical Technology Association'

questions.explanation: NOTA means 'None of the Above'; it allows an elector to register that they do not wish to vote for any of the listed candidates.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is an EVM?

options.A: An Electronic Voting Machine is a device used to record votes electronically in elections conducted under the applicable rules
options.B: An Electronic Voting Machine is a device used to count votes manually
options.C: An Electronic Voting Machine is a device used to print ballot papers
options.D: An Electronic Voting Machine is a device used to verify voter identity

questions.explanation: An Electronic Voting Machine is a device used to record votes electronically in elections conducted under the applicable rules.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is VVPAT?

options.A: Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail is a system that allows voters to verify a printed paper slip corresponding to their vote, displayed for a brief period before it is deposited in a sealed box
options.B: Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail is a system for online voting
options.C: Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail is a system for voter registration
options.D: Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail is a system for counting votes

questions.explanation: Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail is a system that allows voters to verify a printed paper slip corresponding to their vote, displayed for a brief period before it is deposited in a sealed box.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: Which laws are central to the conduct of parliamentary and assembly elections in India?

options.A: The Representation of the People Act, 1950, mainly concerning electoral rolls and related matters, and the Representation of the People Act, 1951, concerning conduct of elections, qualifications, disqualifications and election disputes
options.B: The Indian Penal Code and the Code of Criminal Procedure
options.C: The Companies Act, 2013 and the Contract Act, 1872
options.D: The Constitution of India only

questions.explanation: The Representation of the People Act, 1950, mainly concerning electoral rolls and related matters, and the Representation of the People Act, 1951, concerning conduct of elections, qualifications, disqualifications and election disputes, are central to the conduct of parliamentary and assembly elections in India.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is an election petition?

options.A: An election petition is a legal proceeding challenging an election on grounds and through procedures prescribed by election law
options.B: An election petition is a request by a candidate to stand for election
options.C: An election petition is a request by a voter for a new voting machine
options.D: An election petition is a request by a party for an election symbol

questions.explanation: An election petition is a legal proceeding challenging an election on grounds and through procedures prescribed by election law.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is the secret ballot?

options.A: A secret ballot is a voting method that protects the privacy of a voter's choice
options.B: A secret ballot is a voting method in which voters publicly announce their choice
options.C: A secret ballot is a voting method in which only the wealthy can vote
options.D: A secret ballot is a voting method in which only men can vote

questions.explanation: A secret ballot is a voting method that protects the privacy of a voter's choice.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is a pressure group?

options.A: A pressure group is an organised group that seeks to influence government decisions, laws or public policy without primarily seeking to form the government itself
options.B: A pressure group is an organised group that seeks to form the government
options.C: A pressure group is a constitutional body
options.D: A pressure group is a political party

questions.explanation: A pressure group is an organised group that seeks to influence government decisions, laws or public policy without primarily seeking to form the government itself.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What are the main functions of pressure groups?

options.A: They represent interests, communicate demands, provide information, lobby decision-makers, mobilise citizens, monitor policies and seek changes in public decisions
options.B: They only contest elections
options.C: They only form governments
options.D: They only provide opposition in the legislature

questions.explanation: The main functions of pressure groups include representing interests, communicating demands, providing information, lobbying decision-makers, mobilising citizens, monitoring policies and seeking changes in public decisions.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is lobbying?

options.A: Lobbying is the organised effort to influence public officials or legislators in relation to laws, regulations or government policy
options.B: Lobbying is the process of contesting elections
options.C: Lobbying is the process of forming a government
options.D: Lobbying is the process of registering voters

questions.explanation: Lobbying is the organised effort to influence public officials or legislators in relation to laws, regulations or government policy.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is a sectional or protective pressure group?

options.A: A sectional pressure group seeks to protect the interests of a particular section, profession, occupation or economic group
options.B: A sectional pressure group campaigns for a cause or principle
options.C: A sectional pressure group seeks to form the government
options.D: A sectional pressure group is a constitutional body

questions.explanation: A sectional or protective pressure group seeks to protect the interests of a particular section, profession, occupation or economic group.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is a promotional or cause group?

options.A: A promotional group campaigns for a cause or principle, such as environmental protection, human rights or public health
options.B: A promotional group seeks to protect the interests of a particular profession
options.C: A promotional group seeks to form the government
options.D: A promotional group is a constitutional body

questions.explanation: A promotional or cause group campaigns for a cause or principle, such as environmental protection, human rights or public health.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is an insider pressure group?

options.A: An insider pressure group has regular access to government decision-makers and is often consulted in policy processes
options.B: An insider pressure group has no access to government decision-makers
options.C: An insider pressure group only uses public campaigns
options.D: An insider pressure group only uses litigation

questions.explanation: An insider pressure group has regular access to government decision-makers and is often consulted in policy processes.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is an outsider pressure group?

options.A: An outsider pressure group has limited formal access to government and may rely more on public campaigns, demonstrations or media advocacy
options.B: An outsider pressure group has regular access to government decision-makers
options.C: An outsider pressure group only uses lobbying
options.D: An outsider pressure group only uses consultations

questions.explanation: An outsider pressure group has limited formal access to government and may rely more on public campaigns, demonstrations or media advocacy.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What are examples of pressure groups?

options.A: Trade unions, farmers' organisations, business associations, professional associations, industry bodies, environmental organisations and civil-society groups
options.B: The Election Commission and the Finance Commission
options.C: The Supreme Court and the High Courts
options.D: The Parliament and the State Legislatures

questions.explanation: Examples of pressure groups include trade unions, farmers' organisations, business associations, professional associations, industry bodies, environmental organisations and civil-society groups.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is the difference between a pressure group and a political party?

options.A: A pressure group seeks to influence policy and decisions; a political party seeks to contest elections and obtain or exercise political power
options.B: A pressure group seeks to form the government; a political party seeks to influence policy
options.C: There is no difference between them
options.D: A pressure group is a constitutional body; a political party is a statutory body

questions.explanation: A pressure group seeks to influence policy and decisions; a political party seeks to contest elections and obtain or exercise political power.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is the difference between a pressure group and a social movement?

options.A: A pressure group is generally an organised interest-influencing body; a social movement is broader collective action seeking to promote, resist or reverse social change
options.B: A pressure group is broader collective action; a social movement is an organised interest-influencing body
options.C: There is no difference between them
options.D: A pressure group is a constitutional body; a social movement is a statutory body

questions.explanation: A pressure group is generally an organised interest-influencing body; a social movement is broader collective action seeking to promote, resist or reverse social change.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What methods do pressure groups use?

options.A: Petitions, lobbying, memoranda, public campaigns, research reports, media engagement, demonstrations, strikes, litigation and consultations, subject to law
options.B: Only contesting elections
options.C: Only forming governments
options.D: Only amending the Constitution

questions.explanation: Pressure groups use methods such as petitions, lobbying, memoranda, public campaigns, research reports, media engagement, demonstrations, strikes, litigation and consultations, subject to law.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is corporatism in interest representation?

options.A: Corporatism is an arrangement in which organised interests, such as employer and worker associations, are formally incorporated into policy consultation or negotiation structures
options.B: Corporatism is an arrangement in which only political parties are consulted
options.C: Corporatism is an arrangement in which only the judiciary is consulted
options.D: Corporatism is an arrangement in which only the military is consulted

questions.explanation: Corporatism is an arrangement in which organised interests, such as employer and worker associations, are formally incorporated into policy consultation or negotiation structures.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is public opinion?

options.A: Public opinion is the aggregate of views, attitudes and judgments held by members of the public on matters of common concern
options.B: Public opinion is the view of the government
options.C: Public opinion is the view of the judiciary
options.D: Public opinion is the view of the military

questions.explanation: Public opinion is the aggregate of views, attitudes and judgments held by members of the public on matters of common concern.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What are the main characteristics of public opinion?

options.A: It concerns public issues, is formed through social communication, may be diverse or changing, and can influence political decisions and public policy
options.B: It concerns only private issues
options.C: It is always uniform and unchanging
options.D: It has no influence on political decisions

questions.explanation: The main characteristics of public opinion are that it concerns public issues, is formed through social communication, may be diverse or changing, and can influence political decisions and public policy.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What are the major factors shaping public opinion?

options.A: Family, education, social class, culture, religion, political parties, leaders, media, peer groups, public events and personal experience
options.B: Only the media
options.C: Only political parties
options.D: Only personal experience

questions.explanation: The major factors shaping public opinion include family, education, social class, culture, religion, political parties, leaders, media, peer groups, public events and personal experience.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is the role of mass media in forming public opinion?

options.A: Mass media select, report and interpret public issues, provide information and platforms for debate, and can influence which issues receive public attention
options.B: Mass media have no role in forming public opinion
options.C: Mass media only report private issues
options.D: Mass media only report government decisions

questions.explanation: Mass media select, report and interpret public issues, provide information and platforms for debate, and can influence which issues receive public attention.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is agenda-setting?

options.A: Agenda-setting is the process by which media attention influences which issues people perceive as important, without necessarily determining what they think about those issues
options.B: Agenda-setting is the process by which the government sets its legislative agenda
options.C: Agenda-setting is the process by which the judiciary sets its case list
options.D: Agenda-setting is the process by which political parties select candidates

questions.explanation: Agenda-setting is the process by which media attention influences which issues people perceive as important, without necessarily determining what they think about those issues.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is political socialisation?

options.A: Political socialisation is the process through which individuals acquire political values, beliefs, attitudes and orientations
options.B: Political socialisation is the process through which political parties are registered
options.C: Political socialisation is the process through which elections are conducted
options.D: Political socialisation is the process through which laws are made

questions.explanation: Political socialisation is the process through which individuals acquire political values, beliefs, attitudes and orientations.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is a public opinion poll?

options.A: A public opinion poll is a survey designed to measure the views or preferences of a defined population using a sample
options.B: A public opinion poll is a formal election
options.C: A public opinion poll is a constitutional body
options.D: A public opinion poll is a political party

questions.explanation: A public opinion poll is a survey designed to measure the views or preferences of a defined population using a sample.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is a representative sample?

options.A: A representative sample is a sample selected and structured so that it adequately reflects relevant characteristics of the population being studied
options.B: A representative sample is a sample that includes only the wealthy
options.C: A representative sample is a sample that includes only one community
options.D: A representative sample is a sample that includes only government officials

questions.explanation: A representative sample is a sample selected and structured so that it adequately reflects relevant characteristics of the population being studied.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is sampling error?

options.A: Sampling error is the difference between a sample estimate and the true population value that arises because only a sample, rather than the whole population, is observed
options.B: Sampling error is a mistake made by the interviewer
options.C: Sampling error is a mistake in the question wording
options.D: Sampling error is a mistake in data entry

questions.explanation: Sampling error is the difference between a sample estimate and the true population value that arises because only a sample, rather than the whole population, is observed.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is a biased poll?

options.A: A biased poll is a survey whose design, sampling, wording, collection or analysis systematically distorts the views it seeks to measure
options.B: A biased poll is a survey that uses a representative sample
options.C: A biased poll is a survey that measures the views of the whole population
options.D: A biased poll is a survey conducted by the government

questions.explanation: A biased poll is a survey whose design, sampling, wording, collection or analysis systematically distorts the views it seeks to measure.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is a referendum?

options.A: A referendum is a direct vote by the electorate on a specific public question or proposal
options.B: A referendum is an election of representatives
options.C: A referendum is a meeting of Parliament
options.D: A referendum is a court proceeding

questions.explanation: A referendum is a direct vote by the electorate on a specific public question or proposal.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is a plebiscite?

options.A: A plebiscite is a direct vote of the people on an important political question, often concerning sovereignty or constitutional status; usage varies by country
options.B: A plebiscite is an election of representatives
options.C: A plebiscite is a meeting of Parliament
options.D: A plebiscite is a court proceeding

questions.explanation: A plebiscite is a direct vote of the people on an important political question, often concerning sovereignty or constitutional status; usage varies by country.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is a public hearing?

options.A: A public hearing is a formal process through which members of the public can present views or objections to an authority before a decision
options.B: A public hearing is a court proceeding
options.C: A public hearing is an election
options.D: A public hearing is a meeting of Parliament

questions.explanation: A public hearing is a formal process through which members of the public can present views or objections to an authority before a decision.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is the difference between public opinion and individual opinion?

options.A: Individual opinion is one person's view; public opinion refers to the wider distribution or aggregate of views within a defined public
options.B: Individual opinion refers to the wider distribution of views; public opinion is one person's view
options.C: There is no difference between them
options.D: Public opinion is the view of the government; individual opinion is the view of the people

questions.explanation: Individual opinion is one person's view; public opinion refers to the wider distribution or aggregate of views within a defined public.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: Why is informed public opinion important in a democracy?

options.A: It helps citizens evaluate government, participate in public debate, hold representatives accountable and shape policy priorities
options.B: It helps the government suppress dissent
options.C: It helps the military control politics
options.D: It helps the judiciary make laws

questions.explanation: Informed public opinion is important in a democracy because it helps citizens evaluate government, participate in public debate, hold representatives accountable and shape policy priorities.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is governance?

options.A: Governance is the process and system through which public authority is exercised, decisions are made, resources are managed and public affairs are administered
options.B: Governance is the same as government
options.C: Governance is the same as the legislature
options.D: Governance is the same as the judiciary

questions.explanation: Governance is the process and system through which public authority is exercised, decisions are made, resources are managed and public affairs are administered.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is the difference between government and governance?

options.A: Government refers to formal institutions and office-holders; governance refers more broadly to the processes and relationships through which public decisions are made and implemented, including non-state actors
options.B: Government refers to processes and relationships; governance refers to formal institutions
options.C: There is no difference between them
options.D: Government includes non-state actors; governance includes only state actors

questions.explanation: Government refers to formal institutions and office-holders; governance refers more broadly to the processes and relationships through which public decisions are made and implemented, including non-state actors.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What are commonly recognised principles of good governance?

options.A: Participation, rule of law, transparency, responsiveness, accountability, effectiveness, efficiency, equity, inclusiveness and consensus orientation
options.B: Only transparency and accountability
options.C: Only participation and rule of law
options.D: Only effectiveness and efficiency

questions.explanation: Commonly recognised principles of good governance include participation, rule of law, transparency, responsiveness, accountability, effectiveness, efficiency, equity, inclusiveness and consensus orientation.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is transparency in governance?

options.A: Transparency means that public decisions, procedures, information and reasons are accessible and understandable, subject to lawful limits
options.B: Transparency means that all government information must be secret
options.C: Transparency means that only the government can access information
options.D: Transparency means that courts must disclose all information

questions.explanation: Transparency means that public decisions, procedures, information and reasons are accessible and understandable, subject to lawful limits.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is accountability in governance?

options.A: Accountability means that public officials and institutions must explain and justify their actions and may face scrutiny, correction or consequences
options.B: Accountability means that public officials are above the law
options.C: Accountability means that public officials cannot be questioned
options.D: Accountability means that only the judiciary is accountable

questions.explanation: Accountability means that public officials and institutions must explain and justify their actions and may face scrutiny, correction or consequences.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is responsiveness in governance?

options.A: Responsiveness means that public institutions address citizens' needs and concerns within a reasonable time
options.B: Responsiveness means that public institutions ignore citizens' needs
options.C: Responsiveness means that public institutions take unlimited time to address concerns
options.D: Responsiveness means that only the judiciary addresses citizens' needs

questions.explanation: Responsiveness means that public institutions address citizens' needs and concerns within a reasonable time.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is citizen participation?

options.A: Citizen participation is the involvement of people in public decision-making, implementation, monitoring and evaluation
options.B: Citizen participation is the involvement of people only in elections
options.C: Citizen participation is the involvement of people only in the judiciary
options.D: Citizen participation is the involvement of people only in the military

questions.explanation: Citizen participation is the involvement of people in public decision-making, implementation, monitoring and evaluation.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is decentralisation?

options.A: Decentralisation is the transfer or distribution of authority, responsibilities and resources from central levels to lower levels of government or institutions
options.B: Decentralisation is the concentration of authority at the central level
options.C: Decentralisation is the transfer of authority from lower levels to central levels
options.D: Decentralisation is the abolition of local governments

questions.explanation: Decentralisation is the transfer or distribution of authority, responsibilities and resources from central levels to lower levels of government or institutions.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is deconcentration?

options.A: Deconcentration is the redistribution of administrative responsibilities within the same level of government, usually from central offices to field offices
options.B: Deconcentration is the transfer of authority from central to local governments
options.C: Deconcentration is the transfer of authority from local to central governments
options.D: Deconcentration is the abolition of field offices

questions.explanation: Deconcentration is the redistribution of administrative responsibilities within the same level of government, usually from central offices to field offices.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is delegation?

options.A: Delegation is the transfer of specified decision-making or administrative functions to semi-autonomous bodies or agencies, while ultimate authority may remain with the delegating government
options.B: Delegation is the transfer of ultimate authority to local governments
options.C: Delegation is the concentration of authority at the central level
options.D: Delegation is the abolition of semi-autonomous bodies

questions.explanation: Delegation is the transfer of specified decision-making or administrative functions to semi-autonomous bodies or agencies, while ultimate authority may remain with the delegating government.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is devolution?

options.A: Devolution is the transfer of meaningful powers, functions and resources to elected subnational governments that have a degree of autonomy
options.B: Devolution is the transfer of administrative responsibilities within the same level of government
options.C: Devolution is the concentration of authority at the central level
options.D: Devolution is the abolition of elected subnational governments

questions.explanation: Devolution is the transfer of meaningful powers, functions and resources to elected subnational governments that have a degree of autonomy.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is e-governance?

options.A: E-governance is the use of information and communication technologies by public institutions to deliver services, exchange information, improve administration and facilitate participation
options.B: E-governance is the use of information and communication technologies only by private companies
options.C: E-governance is the use of information and communication technologies only by the judiciary
options.D: E-governance is the use of information and communication technologies only by the military

questions.explanation: E-governance is the use of information and communication technologies by public institutions to deliver services, exchange information, improve administration and facilitate participation.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is the Right to Information Act, 2005?

options.A: It is an Indian law that gives citizens a statutory right to access information held by public authorities, subject to exemptions and procedures
options.B: It is an Indian law that gives citizens a statutory right to access information held by private companies
options.C: It is an Indian law that gives citizens a statutory right to access information held by foreign governments
options.D: It is an Indian law that gives citizens a statutory right to access information held by the judiciary only

questions.explanation: The Right to Information Act, 2005 is an Indian law that gives citizens a statutory right to access information held by public authorities, subject to exemptions and procedures.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is a citizen charter?

options.A: A citizen charter is a public document stating the services an organisation provides, service standards, time limits and grievance-redress mechanisms
options.B: A citizen charter is a constitutional amendment
options.C: A citizen charter is a law passed by Parliament
options.D: A citizen charter is a judicial order

questions.explanation: A citizen charter is a public document stating the services an organisation provides, service standards, time limits and grievance-redress mechanisms.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is a grievance-redress mechanism?

options.A: It is a formal process through which citizens can submit complaints about public services or decisions and seek resolution
options.B: It is a process through which citizens can amend the Constitution
options.C: It is a process through which citizens can elect representatives
options.D: It is a process through which citizens can form political parties

questions.explanation: A grievance-redress mechanism is a formal process through which citizens can submit complaints about public services or decisions and seek resolution.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is the Lokpal?

options.A: The Lokpal is a statutory anti-corruption ombudsman at the Union level established under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013
options.B: The Lokpal is a constitutional court
options.C: The Lokpal is a political party
options.D: The Lokpal is an election commission

questions.explanation: The Lokpal is a statutory anti-corruption ombudsman at the Union level established under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is a Lokayukta?

options.A: A Lokayukta is an anti-corruption or public-grievance ombudsman institution established under the relevant law of a State
options.B: A Lokayukta is a constitutional court at the Union level
options.C: A Lokayukta is a political party
options.D: A Lokayukta is an election commission

questions.explanation: A Lokayukta is an anti-corruption or public-grievance ombudsman institution established under the relevant law of a State.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is the Central Vigilance Commission?

options.A: The CVC is a statutory vigilance institution that exercises functions assigned by law concerning vigilance administration and corruption-related matters in specified central public bodies
options.B: The CVC is a constitutional court
options.C: The CVC is an election commission
options.D: The CVC is a political party

questions.explanation: The Central Vigilance Commission is a statutory vigilance institution that exercises functions assigned by law concerning vigilance administration and corruption-related matters in specified central public bodies.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is the Central Information Commission?

options.A: The CIC is the statutory central information commission established under the Right to Information Act, 2005 to hear appeals and complaints under that Act
options.B: The CIC is a constitutional court
options.C: The CIC is an election commission
options.D: The CIC is a political party

questions.explanation: The Central Information Commission is the statutory central information commission established under the Right to Information Act, 2005 to hear appeals and complaints under that Act.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is sustainable governance?

options.A: Sustainable governance integrates economic, social, institutional and environmental considerations into public decision-making for present and future generations
options.B: Sustainable governance focuses only on economic growth
options.C: Sustainable governance focuses only on environmental protection
options.D: Sustainable governance focuses only on social welfare

questions.explanation: Sustainable governance integrates economic, social, institutional and environmental considerations into public decision-making for present and future generations.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is federalism?

options.A: Federalism is a constitutional system in which governmental powers are divided between a national government and regional governments, with each having constitutionally recognised authority
options.B: Federalism is a system in which all powers are concentrated in the central government
options.C: Federalism is a system in which there is no central government
options.D: Federalism is a system in which local governments have no powers

questions.explanation: Federalism is a constitutional system in which governmental powers are divided between a national government and regional governments, with each having constitutionally recognised authority.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What are the main features of federalism?

options.A: A written and supreme constitution, division of powers, at least two levels of government, constitutional procedures for dispute resolution and an independent judiciary or other constitutional mechanism
options.B: An unwritten constitution and concentration of powers
options.C: A single level of government
options.D: No judicial review

questions.explanation: The main features of federalism include a written and supreme constitution, division of powers, at least two levels of government, constitutional procedures for dispute resolution and an independent judiciary or other constitutional mechanism.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is dual federalism?

options.A: Dual federalism describes a model in which national and regional governments operate in relatively distinct spheres of authority
options.B: Dual federalism describes a model in which national and regional governments collaborate closely
options.C: Dual federalism describes a model in which regional governments have no authority
options.D: Dual federalism describes a model in which there is only one level of government

questions.explanation: Dual federalism describes a model in which national and regional governments operate in relatively distinct spheres of authority.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is cooperative federalism?

options.A: Cooperative federalism emphasises coordination and collaboration between different levels of government in policy-making and implementation
options.B: Cooperative federalism emphasises competition among States
options.C: Cooperative federalism emphasises the concentration of powers in the central government
options.D: Cooperative federalism emphasises the abolition of state governments

questions.explanation: Cooperative federalism emphasises coordination and collaboration between different levels of government in policy-making and implementation.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is competitive federalism?

options.A: Competitive federalism describes competition among States or regions to improve governance, attract investment or achieve development outcomes
options.B: Competitive federalism describes collaboration among States
options.C: Competitive federalism describes the concentration of powers in the central government
options.D: Competitive federalism describes the abolition of state governments

questions.explanation: Competitive federalism describes competition among States or regions to improve governance, attract investment or achieve development outcomes.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is fiscal federalism?

options.A: Fiscal federalism concerns the division of taxation powers, public expenditure responsibilities and financial transfers among different levels of government
options.B: Fiscal federalism concerns only the division of taxation powers
options.C: Fiscal federalism concerns only public expenditure responsibilities
options.D: Fiscal federalism concerns only financial transfers

questions.explanation: Fiscal federalism concerns the division of taxation powers, public expenditure responsibilities and financial transfers among different levels of government.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: Is India a federation?

options.A: India has a federal constitutional structure with a strong Union and several unitary features; the Supreme Court has described the Constitution's federal character as part of its basic structure
options.B: India is a purely unitary state
options.C: India is a confederation
options.D: India is not a federation in any sense

questions.explanation: India has a federal constitutional structure with a strong Union and several unitary features; the Supreme Court has described the Constitution's federal character as part of its basic structure.

questions.question: Which article describes India as a Union of States?

questions.question: Which schedule distributes legislative subjects between the Union and States?

questions.question: What are the three legislative lists in the Seventh Schedule?

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: Who can legislate on subjects in the Union List?

options.A: Parliament has exclusive ordinary legislative competence over Union List subjects, subject to constitutional provisions
options.B: State Legislatures have exclusive competence over Union List subjects
options.C: Both Parliament and State Legislatures have equal competence over Union List subjects
options.D: Local governments have exclusive competence over Union List subjects

questions.explanation: Parliament has exclusive ordinary legislative competence over Union List subjects, subject to constitutional provisions.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: Who can legislate on subjects in the State List?

options.A: State Legislatures ordinarily legislate on State List subjects, subject to constitutional exceptions that permit Parliament to legislate in specified circumstances
options.B: Parliament has exclusive competence over State List subjects
options.C: Both Parliament and State Legislatures have equal competence over State List subjects
options.D: Local governments have exclusive competence over State List subjects

questions.explanation: State Legislatures ordinarily legislate on State List subjects, subject to constitutional exceptions that permit Parliament to legislate in specified circumstances.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: Who can legislate on subjects in the Concurrent List?

options.A: Both Parliament and State Legislatures can legislate on Concurrent List subjects; Article 254 generally deals with repugnancy between central and state laws
options.B: Only Parliament can legislate on Concurrent List subjects
options.C: Only State Legislatures can legislate on Concurrent List subjects
options.D: Only local governments can legislate on Concurrent List subjects

questions.explanation: Both Parliament and State Legislatures can legislate on Concurrent List subjects; Article 254 generally deals with repugnancy between central and state laws.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What happens when a State law conflicts with a Parliamentary law on a Concurrent List subject?

options.A: Under Article 254, the Parliamentary law generally prevails to the extent of repugnancy, subject to the constitutional exception where a State law reserved for and receiving Presidential assent may prevail in that State; Parliament can later override it
options.B: The State law always prevails
options.C: Both laws are automatically void
options.D: The Supreme Court decides which law prevails in each case

questions.explanation: Under Article 254, the Parliamentary law generally prevails to the extent of repugnancy, subject to the constitutional exception where a State law reserved for and receiving Presidential assent may prevail in that State; Parliament can later override it.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: Which article provides for Parliament to legislate on a State List matter in the national interest if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution?

questions.explanation: Article 249 provides for Parliament to legislate on a State List matter in the national interest if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution.

questions.question: Which article allows Parliament to legislate on State List matters during a Proclamation of Emergency?

options.A: Article 250
options.B: Article 249
options.C: Article 252
options.D: Article 253

questions.explanation: Article 250 allows Parliament to legislate on State List matters during a Proclamation of Emergency.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: Which article provides for Parliament to legislate for two or more States by consent?

options.A: Article 252
options.B: Article 249
options.C: Article 250
options.D: Article 253

questions.explanation: Article 252 provides for Parliament to legislate for two or more States by consent.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: Which article provides for Parliament to implement international agreements through legislation?

options.A: Article 253
options.B: Article 249
options.C: Article 250
options.D: Article 252

questions.explanation: Article 253 provides for Parliament to implement international agreements through legislation.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: Which article deals with the Inter-State Council?

options.A: Article 263
options.B: Article 262
options.C: Article 280
options.D: Article 279A

questions.explanation: Article 263 deals with the Inter-State Council.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is the Finance Commission's role in federal relations?

options.A: It recommends specified tax devolution and grants-in-aid arrangements between the Union and States under Article 280
options.B: It conducts elections
options.C: It audits government expenditure
options.D: It appoints judges

questions.explanation: The Finance Commission recommends specified tax devolution and grants-in-aid arrangements between the Union and States under Article 280.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is the GST Council?

options.A: The GST Council is a constitutional body under Article 279A that makes recommendations on key aspects of the Goods and Services Tax

questions.question: Which Constitutional Amendment introduced the GST Council?

options.B: The 100th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2015

questions.explanation: The 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 introduced the GST Council.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is an inter-state river water dispute?

options.A: It is a dispute between States concerning the use, distribution or control of waters of an inter-state river or river valley
options.B: It is a dispute between the Union and a State over taxation
options.C: It is a dispute between two countries over a river
options.D: It is a dispute between local governments over water supply

questions.explanation: An inter-state river water dispute is a dispute between States concerning the use, distribution or control of waters of an inter-state river or river valley.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: Which article empowers Parliament to provide for adjudication of inter-state river water disputes?

options.A: Article 262
options.B: Article 263
options.C: Article 280
options.D: Article 279A

questions.explanation: Article 262 empowers Parliament to provide for adjudication of inter-state river water disputes.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is President's Rule in a State?

options.A: President's Rule is the constitutional arrangement under Article 356 for a situation in which the government of a State cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution, subject to constitutional safeguards and judicial review
options.B: President's Rule is the constitutional arrangement under Article 352 for a national emergency
options.C: President's Rule is the constitutional arrangement under Article 360 for a financial emergency
options.D: President's Rule is the constitutional arrangement under Article 368 for constitutional amendments

questions.explanation: President's Rule is the constitutional arrangement under Article 356 for a situation in which the government of a State cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution, subject to constitutional safeguards and judicial review.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is the role of the Governor in Indian federalism?

options.A: The Governor is the constitutional head of a State, appointed by the President, and performs functions under the Constitution, normally acting on the aid and advice of the State Council of Ministers except where discretion is constitutionally permitted
options.B: The Governor is the elected head of a State
options.C: The Governor is appointed by the Chief Justice of India
options.D: The Governor is appointed by the State Legislature

questions.explanation: The Governor is the constitutional head of a State, appointed by the President, and performs functions under the Constitution, normally acting on the aid and advice of the State Council of Ministers except where discretion is constitutionally permitted.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is asymmetric federalism?

options.A: Asymmetric federalism is a federal arrangement in which different constituent units have different powers, protections or institutional arrangements
options.B: Asymmetric federalism is a federal arrangement in which all constituent units have identical powers
options.C: Asymmetric federalism is a federal arrangement in which there is only one constituent unit
options.D: Asymmetric federalism is a federal arrangement in which there is no central government

questions.explanation: Asymmetric federalism is a federal arrangement in which different constituent units have different powers, protections or institutional arrangements.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is the difference between federal and unitary government?

options.A: Federal government constitutionally divides authority between levels of government; unitary government places ultimate legal authority in the central government, which may delegate powers
options.B: Federal government places ultimate authority in the central government; unitary government divides authority between levels
options.C: There is no difference between them
options.D: Federal government has no constitution; unitary government has a constitution

questions.explanation: Federal government constitutionally divides authority between levels of government; unitary government places ultimate legal authority in the central government, which may delegate powers.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is local government?

options.A: Local government is the system of elected or constituted institutions that administer public affairs and provide services at village, town or city level
options.B: Local government is the system of central government institutions
options.C: Local government is the system of state government institutions
options.D: Local government is the system of international institutions

questions.explanation: Local government is the system of elected or constituted institutions that administer public affairs and provide services at village, town or city level.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: Why is local self-government important?

options.A: It brings decision-making closer to residents, supports participation, responds to local needs, improves accountability and enables decentralised planning and service delivery
options.B: It concentrates power in the central government
options.C: It reduces citizen participation
options.D: It increases the power of the judiciary

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: What is a Gram Sabha?

questions.question: What are the three tiers of Panchayati Raj in the general three-tier structure?

options.B: Gram Panchayat, Municipal Council and Municipal Corporation
options.C: Gram Sabha, Gram Panchayat and Zilla Parishad

questions.explanation: The three tiers of Panchayati Raj in the general three-tier structure are Gram Panchayat at village level, intermediate-level Panchayat (often called Taluk or Panchayat Samiti) and Zilla Panchayat or Zilla Parishad at district level; constitutional exceptions apply to States with a population not exceeding 20 lakh.

questions.question: Which part of the Constitution deals with Municipalities?

questions.question: Which article provides for the Finance Commission?

questions.question: Which article provides for the GST Council?

questions.question: Which article provides that no person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law?

questions.question: Which article provides for All-India Services?

questions.question: Which article provides for Public Service Commissions for the Union and States?

options.B: Article 312

questions.explanation: Article 315 provides for Public Service Commissions for the Union and States.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: Which article vests the superintendence, direction and control of elections in the Election Commission?

options.B: Article 315
options.C: Article 326
options.D: Article 352

questions.explanation: Article 324 vests the superintendence, direction and control of elections in the Election Commission.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: Which article provides for elections to the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies on the basis of adult suffrage?

options.B: Article 324
options.C: Article 315
options.D: Article 352

questions.explanation: Article 326 provides for elections to the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies on the basis of adult suffrage.

questions.question: Which article provides for the Proclamation of Emergency?

options.D: Article 326

questions.explanation: Article 352 provides for the Proclamation of Emergency.

questions.subject: Political Science
questions.question: Which article provides for provisions in case of failure of constitutional machinery in States?

options.B: Article 352
